sections.h2: Where is Boone County, Indiana, and how is it laid out?
sections.html:
Boone County sits near the middle of Indiana, northwest of Indianapolis, with Lebanon as the county seat. The county runs about 24 miles east to west and 17.5 miles north to south, and covers 423.25 square miles, almost all of it land.

Its neighbors are Clinton County to the north, Hamilton to the east, Marion to the southeast, Hendricks to the south and Montgomery to the west. Sugar Creek drains the west side, Big Raccoon Creek the southwest and Eagle Creek the southeast. The highest ground is a small hill, 984 feet above sea level, about two miles northeast of Lebanon.

For a seller, the layout matters because the county is really two housing markets under one tax office. The southeast corner is suburban Zionsville, about 15 miles northwest of downtown Indianapolis. The rest is Lebanon, smaller towns and farm country, where about two thirds of the land has been cultivated.

sections.h2: How did Boone County get started?
sections.html:
The legislature created Boone County on April 1, 1830, and it was organized in 1831. It was named for the frontiersman Daniel Boone, and Jamestown served as the first county seat before Lebanon was chosen as the permanent one.

Lebanon itself was established on April 30, 1830. A pioneer reportedly picked the name because a stand of hickory trees reminded him of the Biblical cedars of Lebanon. The first post office opened in 1832, the community became a town in 1853 and a city in 1875.

Zionsville has a different story. It was laid out in 1852 when the railroad was extended to the site and was named for settler William Zion. It incorporated in 1866, and the old rail corridor is now the Big-4 Rail Trail. Many older homes in both places date from these railroad and farm eras, which is worth knowing if you own a house that has never had its wiring, plumbing or foundation updated.

sections.h2: What does the Boone County economy look like?
sections.html:
Boone County combines agriculture, manufacturing, distribution and fast-growing technology projects, with Lebanon at the center of most of them. Large employers in Lebanon include the Lebanon Community School Corporation, the U.S. headquarters of Festool and Skjodt-Barrett, and plants run by Hendrickson International, DS Smith, Kuraray, Kauffman Engineering, Maplehurst Bakeries and D-A Lubricant Company.

Distribution centers there serve CNH Parts and Services, Subaru of America, Continental Tire the Americas and Hachette Book Group USA. Witham Health Services runs medical facilities in the city.

The biggest change is the LEAP Research and Innovation District, which covers more than 9,000 acres set aside for technology and manufacturing. Eli Lilly plans a $9 billion facility there to make active ingredients for tirzepatide, with production slated to begin in late 2026. When the district is complete it is expected to employ around 50,000 people.

Projects of that size pull on local housing in two directions. Some owners expect strong demand and wait. Others, especially heirs, landlords and owners with deferred repairs, would rather sell now and skip the preparation. Both groups still owe the same tax bill until closing.

sections.h2: How do Boone County property tax payments work?
sections.html:
Boone County property tax is paid to the county treasurer in two equal installments, due May 10 and November 10 under Indiana law. The state tax calendar lists the 2026 dates as May 11 and November 10, because May 10 fell on a Sunday.

The treasurer's office is on the second floor of the county courthouse in downtown Lebanon, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., and closed on legal holidays and Election Day. Treasurer Nikki Baldwin can be reached at 765-482-2880.

  • In person: cash, personal checks, cashier checks, certified checks and money orders. Cards are accepted only online.
  • By mail: payable to Boone County Treasurer, 209 Courthouse Square, Lebanon, IN 46052. The envelope must carry a post office postmark by the due date, and a postage meter date does not count.
  • Online and phone: through the county's payment portal or 1-877-886-1892. Cards cost 2.95% with a $1.95 minimum. An ACH payment has a flat $0.95 fee.

The treasurer warns against paying by bank bill pay check, because those envelopes usually do not receive a post office postmark. If you are selling, pay the bill directly or give the title company a copy of it.

sections.h2: How does a property tax appeal work in Boone County?
sections.html:
You start a Boone County appeal by filing Form 130 with the Assessor's Office. For 2026, the county mailed assessment notices (Form 11) on April 28 and set the appeal deadline at June 15, 2026, printed at the top of the notice.

Before appealing, check your property record card. If it lists the wrong square footage, bathroom count, outbuildings or basement, the county offers a separate correction of error. Filing is allowed by email to assessmentappeal@co.boone.in.us, by mail or in person, and you should attach evidence. Someone other than the owner or a family member needs a signed power of attorney.

  1. The Assessor reviews your appeal after the deadline and contacts you for a preliminary hearing.
  2. If you cannot agree, the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals (PTABOA) hears the case, usually on a Wednesday, with notice by mail.
  3. You get a Form 115 with the board's decision.
  4. If you disagree, file Form 131 with the Indiana Board of Tax Review and send the Assessor a copy.
  5. After that decision you can seek review in the Indiana Tax Court.

The county warns that an appeal can leave your value higher, lower or unchanged. State guidance says the PTABOA hearing must occur within 180 days of filing, with at least 30 days of notice. See the Boone County Assessor appeal page for current forms.

sections.h2: What happens to taxes and deductions when a Boone County house sells?
sections.html:
Indiana requires a sales disclosure form signed by the buyer and seller before the deed is filed with the county auditor. The county assessor reviews it first, and each parcel needs its own form, with a single exception for contiguous parcels inside one taxing district.

Taxes are billed in arrears, so a spring or fall installment can fall due around your closing date. Title companies normally split the bill between buyer and seller by closing date, which you should confirm with your closing agent.

The homestead deduction also changes hands. Under the version of the statute we reviewed, the standard deduction is 60% of assessed value, up to $48,000 for assessments after 2022, and a new owner who buys after the assessment date can qualify by filing the statement or a sales disclosure form with the assessor by December 31 of the purchase year. The statute was amended effective January 1, 2025, so check with the Auditor for the current figure.

sections.h2: What if Boone County property tax goes unpaid?
sections.html:
A late payment adds a penalty under Indiana law. Paying within 30 days of the due date adds 5% of the delinquent tax if there is no earlier delinquency on the parcel. In every other case the penalty is 10%.

Later installments can bring additional 10% penalties, and the penalties apply to the principal owed. Payments go first to the tax and then to the penalty. Past that point the parcel can be offered at a county tax sale, and Indiana owners generally have one year to redeem. Confirm timing with the Boone County Treasurer before assuming any date.

A house with a delinquent bill can still be sold. The unpaid tax and penalty are settled from the proceeds at closing, which is one reason sellers with several years of back tax often prefer a direct cash sale over listing.

sections.h2: What do Boone County sellers usually run into?
sections.html:
Most Boone County sellers face one of a few situations: a house that needs work, an inherited property, a tenant, or a timing problem. The county's housing stock ranges widely, from older homes in Lebanon and small towns to newer subdivisions around Zionsville, where the median owner-occupied home value was reported at $406,800 in the 2016 to 2020 American Community Survey.

  • Check your Form 11 value against what you would accept in a sale.
  • Pull the property record card and fix any errors before they affect a buyer's review.
  • Keep the latest tax bill, mortgage payoff and any estate papers ready.
  • Ask the treasurer for the current balance before scheduling a closing.

If you want to skip repairs, showings and appraisal delays, a cash offer for a Boone County house can close on your timeline, with tax proration handled at the title company.

faqs.q: When are Boone County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Boone County property taxes are due in two equal installments on May 10 and November 10 under Indiana law. In 2026 the state calendar listed May 11 and November 10, since May 10 was a Sunday. Mailed payments must be postmarked by the due date.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Boone County property tax in person?
faqs.a: You pay at the Boone County Treasurer's office on the second floor of the courthouse in downtown Lebanon. It is open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., except legal holidays and Election Day. Cash, checks, cashier checks and money orders are accepted in person, and cards are online only.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Boone County assessment?
faqs.a: The 2026 deadline was June 15, 2026, and notices were mailed April 28. File Form 130 with the Boone County Assessor, by email, mail or in person. Check the date printed on your own Form 11 each year.

faqs.q: How much is the late penalty on Indiana property tax?
faqs.a: The penalty is 5% of the delinquent amount if you pay within 30 days of the due date and have no earlier delinquency on the parcel. Otherwise it is 10%. Additional 10% penalties can attach to later installments.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Boone County house with unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes, you can sell a Boone County house with taxes still owed. The balance, plus any penalty, is paid from your proceeds at closing. Ask the treasurer for an exact payoff before the closing date.
